text: vur_reflux · vesicoureteric reflux · ureter · vesicoureteral_reflux · a micturating cystourethrogram (mcug) shows contrast refluxing from the bladder back up the ureter (± into the kidney), graded i–v by how high it goes and how dilated the system becomes. · reflux is intermittent — a single static image can miss it; image during voiding · high-grade reflux with a dilated, clubbed system risks renal scarring (check with dmsa) · it is a paediatric-predominant diagnosis — context matters · mcug · contrast refluxing up both ureters into dilated systems

label: Three Geometries of Failure
text: three geometries of failure · where a patient feels the problem is often not where the problem is. this page gives you one question to ask first, before you think about which disease it could be: what shape of structure has failed? what you'll be able to do sort a body structure into one of three shapes: layers , conduits or networks . ask the question that shape needs: which depth , which station , or which territory . use the answer to pick where to look next on exam and imaging. this is a memory aid for localising a problem. it sits on top of the usual history, exam and differential diagnosis; it doesn't replace them.

label: Three patients, one shift
text: three patients, one shift · each of these patients points to one place. in each, the problem is somewhere else, and the shape of the structure tells you where. a lump in the groin they point to a bulge under the skin that comes out when they cough. the problem is a weak spot several layers deeper, in the abdominal wall. ask which depth? pain in the flank they point to the side of the back, where the kidney is. the problem is a stone lower down in the ureter. the kidney is swollen because urine can't get past. ask which station? a weak right arm they point to the arm, and words that won't come out right. the problem is one blocked artery branch in the left side of the brain. ask which territory? the symptom shows up where the body can feel or notice it. the cause sits wherever the structure actually broke. the shape of the structure tells you how to get from one to the other. 1

label: Layers
text: layers · the question: which depth? everyday picture a wall in a house: paint, plaster, drywall, insulation, studs. a damp patch shows on the paint, but the leak is in a pipe behind the drywall. repainting won't fix it. you have to find the layer where it starts. skin (surface) fat muscle and its sheath transversalis fascia: the weak spot peritoneum bowel × symptom: a bulge felt at the skin cause: a gap four layers down all the layers are there at once, stacked at the same spot. the bulge appears at the top; the gap is deeper. in the body the abdominal wall, skin, the meninges around the brain, the wall of the bowel or bladder, the eye's cornea. anywhere tissue is stacked in sheets. how to find the problem start at the symptom on the surface. go one layer deeper and ask: is this layer normal? keep going until you reach the first layer that isn't. that's the lesion. treat at that depth, not at the surface.

label: Worked case: indirect inguinal hernia
text: worked case: indirect inguinal hernia · a 45-year-old man has a groin bulge that appears when he coughs or lifts. the skin over it is normal, so the problem is deeper than the skin. the bulge follows the inguinal canal toward the scrotum, which points to the deep inguinal ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia. repair reinforces that deep layer (usually with mesh). nothing is done to the skin except the incision. common trap: treating the layer you can see. a skin ointment for a bulge, or a cream for a wound that's really tunnelling deeper, leaves the real defect untouched. 2

label: Conduits
text: conduits · the question: which station? everyday picture a kitchen sink. if the pipe under it clogs, the sink fills up (above the clog) and nothing reaches the drain (below it). you don't fix it by scrubbing the sink. you find the clog, and the full sink tells you it's somewhere below. 1 kidney makes urine 2 ureter carries it 3 bladder stores it 4 control sphincters 5 outlet prostate, urethra × urine flows this way → swollen above the block (hydronephrosis) quiet below the block stone where the ureter meets the bladder the five stations of the urinary tract, as used throughout this reference. everything above the block swells; everything below goes quiet. in the body the urinary tract, the bile ducts, the gut, the airway, the flow of fluid around the brain. anything with a start, a series of steps, and an exit. how to find the problem find where the flow visibly stops (no output, a full bladder, a swollen kidney on ultrasound). look upstream: those stations are swollen from back-pressure. look downstream: those stations are empty or quiet. the lesion is at the boundary between swollen and empty. treat there.

label: Worked case: a stone in the ureter
text: worked case: a stone in the ureter · a 38-year-old has waves of severe flank pain spreading to the groin. ultrasound shows a swollen kidney (station 1 distended), so the block is below the kidney. ct shows a dilated ureter down to a 6 mm stone where it enters the bladder, and a normal ureter below it. station 2 is the lesion. treatment is aimed at the stone: let it pass, or remove it with a scope. the kidney recovers once urine can flow again. common trap: treating the swollen station. the kidney hurts and looks abnormal, but it's the victim. the cause is the first station where flow stopped. 3

label: Networks
text: networks · the question: which territory? everyday picture the electrical circuits in a house. when one breaker trips, one room goes dark and the rest stay on. the dark room tells you which breaker it was. you read the problem from the pattern of what's missing. s source (heart) × territory lost face, arm, speech other branches still working one blocked branch one branch fails; only the area it supplies stops working. the shape of that area points back to the branch. in the body arteries and veins, nerves, the lymphatics, the branching airways. anything where one source fans out to supply many separate areas. how to find the problem map exactly what's missing: which muscles are weak, which skin is numb, which part is cold or pale. ask which single branch supplies all of that, and nothing else. the lesion is at that branch point, upstream of the whole affected area. treat the branch: reopen it, or protect what it supplies while collaterals take over.

label: Worked case: a stroke
text: worked case: a stroke · a 72-year-old suddenly can't lift their right arm, the right side of the face droops, and they can't find words. right face, right arm and language together is one territory: the left side of the brain supplied by the left middle cerebral artery. the legs and vision are spared, which fits one branch rather than the whole brain. ct angiography confirms a blocked left middle cerebral artery. treatment aims to reopen it, and every minute counts. common trap: examining the part that stopped working. the weak arm is normal; the territory map is what points you to the brain.

label: The cheat sheet
text: the cheat sheet · if you remember one thing from this page, remember this table. shape ask find it by treat layers which depth? going deeper until a layer is abnormal. at that depth, not at the surface. conduits which station? finding where swollen meets empty. at the station where flow first stopped. networks which territory? mapping what's missing, then the branch that supplies it. at the branch, or support what it supplied.

label: Most organs mix the shapes
text: most organs mix the shapes · real organs combine all three. naming which shape a problem belongs to tells you which question to ask about it. kidney network a clot in a renal artery branch kills a wedge of kidney. conduit a stone blocks the outflow. layers in some kidney diseases the filter itself leaks protein, at one layer of its wall. lung conduit a mucus plug blocks an airway. network a pulmonary embolus cuts off a branch of the blood supply. layers pneumonia fills the air sacs. skin layers a burn or a pressure injury is graded by how deep it goes. network red streaks running up a limb follow the lymphatic channels.

label: Try it
text: try it · name the shape and the question before you open each answer. 1 a 74-year-old man hasn't passed urine for 10 hours. his bladder is palpable up to his umbilicus. show conduit · which station? the bladder (station 3) is full, so the block is below it: the outlet (station 5), most often an enlarged prostate. a catheter bypasses the block. 2 two burns side by side: one is red, blistered and very painful; the other is white, leathery and painless. show layers · which depth? the painful one is partial thickness: the nerve endings in the dermis still work. the painless one has gone through the full thickness of the skin and destroyed them, so it is deeper and more serious. 3 after an elbow injury, the little finger and half the ring finger are numb, and finger-spreading is weak. show network · which territory? that exact sensory and muscle pattern is the territory of the ulnar nerve, which runs behind the elbow. the lesion is at the elbow, not in the hand. 4 yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, pale stools. ultrasound shows widened bile ducts inside the liver. show conduit · which station? ducts are swollen above a block, and pale stools mean bile isn't reaching the gut below it. look at the common bile duct for a stone or a tumour. 5 a cold, pale left foot and calf. the femoral pulse at the groin is normal; there are no pulses below the knee. show network · which territory? normal above, missing below: the blocked branch sits between the groin and the knee, likely the femoral or popliteal artery. this is an emergency. 6 a painful bulge near an old abdominal surgery scar, worse when standing. show layers · which depth? an incisional hernia: the skin healed, but the fascia underneath didn't hold. the repair is at the fascia.

label: Where this model stops working
text: where this model stops working · whole-body problems. sepsis, diabetes, low sodium or a drug side effect don't live at one depth, station or branch. use the usual approach for those. it finds the place, not the cause. knowing the block is in the ureter doesn't tell you it's a stone rather than a tumour. that's the next step. organs mix shapes. if one shape doesn't explain everything you see, try another, or two together. it's a teaching frame. clinicians already localise this way, especially in neurology. this page just names the three patterns so they are easier to learn.

label: Words used on this page
text: words used on this page · lesion the spot where the structure is damaged or blocked. fascia a tough sheet of connective tissue; the transversalis fascia lines the inside of the abdominal wall. hydronephrosis a kidney swollen with urine that can't drain. ureter the tube that carries urine from each kidney to the bladder. territory the area of tissue that one artery or nerve branch supplies. collaterals back-up vessels that can take over some of a blocked branch's job.

label: The Urinary Tract — A Conduit
text: the urinary tract — a conduit · urine is made in the kidney and leaves through the urethra, passing five stations on the way. it flows one way only. the patient feels the problem at the exit, but the cause is often further up. your job is to find which part failed first.

label: How to think about the urinary tract
text: how to think about the urinary tract · the urinary tract is a conduit : a one-way tube, like a garden hose, and the second of the three geometries . so the question is different from the abdominal wall. you don't ask "how deep is the problem?" you ask "where along the tube did the flow first stop?" tubes go wrong in a few typical ways. block one and pressure builds above the block while nothing comes out the end. let bacteria in and the infection travels down with the flow and climbs back up against it. damage the wall and urine leaks out where it shouldn't. the pattern tells you where the problem is. the one rule to remember start where the flow visibly stops: that's where the patient notices it. then work back up the tube . everything above the block shows damage from back-pressure (a widened ureter, a swollen bladder, an injured kidney). everything below is empty or quiet (nothing coming out, shrunken from disuse). the problem sits where the swelling ends and the quiet begins. the urinary tract, in the body. kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra (ringed by the prostate) → exit. every complaint at the exit points back to somewhere along this path. keep the picture in mind while reading about each part below. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract .

label: The five stations, kidney to outlet
text: the five stations, kidney to outlet · they are numbered in the direction urine flows: the kidney makes it, the outlet lets it out. each part has one job and a typical way of going wrong. 1 production kidney 2 transport ureter 3 storage bladder · detrusor 4 control sphincters · nerves 5 outlet prostate · urethra direction of flow · kidney → outlet 5 stations · urine flows one way · work back up from where it stops 1

label: Production · kidney
text: production · kidney · the glomerulus filters the blood. the tubules concentrate what's filtered. the collecting ducts deliver urine to the calyces and the renal pelvis, the kidney's own drainage system.

label: When it goes wrong:
text: when it goes wrong: · blood in the urine (hematuria) from the filter or kidney tissue. kidney infection (pyelonephritis). kidney masses. acute kidney injury (aki) from prerenal, intrarenal or postrenal causes. a swollen kidney (hydronephrosis) when the ureter is blocked. 2

label: Transport · ureter
text: transport · ureter · a 25 cm muscular tube. waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis) push urine along, even against gravity. it narrows naturally in three places where stones often stick: where it leaves the kidney (ureteropelvic junction, upj), where it crosses the pelvic brim, and where it enters the bladder (ureterovesical junction, uvj).

label: Storage · bladder
text: storage · bladder · a stretchy reservoir. its most important property is that it holds urine at low pressure. the trigone (the base of the bladder) is rich in sensory nerves. the bladder muscle (detrusor) contracts on command to empty it.

label: Control · sphincters & nerves
text: control · sphincters & nerves · two gates. the internal sphincter (smooth muscle, sympathetic α1, not under conscious control) sits at the bladder neck. the external sphincter (striated muscle, pudendal nerve, under conscious control) sits at the membranous urethra. the pons in the brainstem coordinates them.

label: Outlet · prostate & urethra
text: outlet · prostate & urethra · the exit tube. in men it runs through the prostate, a solid gland wrapped around the tube. narrowing, squeezing and blockage all happen here.

label: Inside the kidney: where the problem sits decides the disease
text: inside the kidney: where the problem sits decides the disease · for the patient, this means two people with "a kidney problem" can need completely different doctors. the kidney is the first stop of the tract, but inside it urine also flows along its own short path, from filter to drain. it's worth one close look, because problems inside the kidney behave differently from problems anywhere else in the tract. g glomerulus filtration t tubule concentration cd collecting duct final regulation c calyx gathering p pelvis → ureter flow inside the kidney urine flows one way inside the kidney too · where it fails decides the disease where the problem sits inside the kidney changes the disease completely. a problem in the glomerulus is one kind of disease (protein in the urine, nephritic syndromes). a problem in the tubules is another (the kidney can't concentrate urine, acute kidney injury). a problem in the collecting ducts, calyx or pelvis is a urology problem (stones in a calyx, a blockage where the pelvis meets the ureter at the upj). same organ, three places, three different specialties. how the three geometries meet in the kidney seen from the urinary tract, the kidney is the first stop of a tube. inside, it is a filter made of nephrons stacked side by side (layers), fed by a branching tree of blood vessels (a network). that is why a kidney can fail in three different ways: disease of the kidney tissue (a layer problem), a blood-supply event (a network problem, e.g. a renal infarct), and a blocked drainage system (a conduit problem, e.g. a stone). each has a different specialist, a different test and a different fix. the kidney (station 1), cut in half. the cortex and medulla make urine; the calyces gather it; the pelvis hands it to the ureter. a blockage anywhere below backs urine up into this space, flattening the calyces (hydronephrosis), thinning the cortex (chronic damage), and in the end stopping the nephrons from working. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract .

label: Filling and emptying: the two phases of the bladder
text: filling and emptying: the two phases of the bladder · for the patient, this is why "i leak" and "i can't go" are different problems. the bladder (station 3) and its control gates, the sphincters and nerves (station 4), work as a team. at any moment they are either filling or emptying, never both. a centre in the brainstem, the pontine micturition centre, switches between the two. phase bladder muscle (detrusor) internal sphincter external sphincter storage sympathetic dominant (t10–l2) relaxed (β3) — bladder fills at low pressure closed (α1) tonic contraction (pudendal) voiding parasympathetic dominant (s2–s4) contracts (m3) opens reflexively voluntary relaxation three things have to be true for voiding to work: the bladder muscle has to squeeze hard enough, both sphincters have to open, and the kidneys and ureters have to have delivered urine to empty. if the timing is lost, and the bladder squeezes against a closed sphincter (dyssynergia), you get high pressure and no flow. to the kidneys, that pressure is the same as a blocked bladder outlet , and it damages the ureters and kidneys in the same way.

label: What keeps the bladder working normally
text: what keeps the bladder working normally · low pressure while filling. the bladder muscle stretches to hold >400 ml with almost no rise in pressure. high pressure while filling is abnormal: it pushes back up the ureters and damages the kidneys. sphincters and bladder in step. when the bladder muscle squeezes, the sphincters open. lose this and the patient pushes at high pressure with no flow. feeling matches volume. first urge at ~150 ml, strong urge at ~300 ml, capacity ~400–500 ml. if the feeling doesn't match the volume, suspect a problem with the bladder's sensory nerves. a simpler way to sort symptoms most bladder and outlet symptoms come from one of three problems: storing (urgency, frequency, leaking: the bladder), emptying (hesitancy, weak stream, retention: the control gates or the outlet), or timing (dribbling after voiding, high-pressure low-flow: the control gates and nerves). pick the group first. the list of possible causes shrinks straight away.

label: Four ways the urinary tract goes wrong
text: four ways the urinary tract goes wrong · four kinds of problem explain almost everything. for each one: where the problem actually is, where the patient notices it, and what the back-pressure above it looks like. kind of problem where the problem is where the patient notices it what you see above it blockage stone, bph, stricture, tumor, clot wherever the tube narrows (most often the ureter or the outlet) nothing or little comes out (weak stream, no urine), or pain where the tube is swollen above the block swelling above the block: a swollen kidney (hydronephrosis) if the ureter is blocked, a swollen bladder if the outlet is infection cystitis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis wherever bacteria settle (kidney, bladder, or outlet) painful urination (dysuria) at the outlet; whole-body signs if the kidney is involved vital signs change with how far up the infection is. bladder infection (cystitis): no fever. kidney infection (pyelonephritis): fever, unwell. same family of bacteria, two places, two diseases. nerve problems (neurogenic) spinal cord injury (sci), ms, diabetes, stroke outside the tract: brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerve the bladder and its control gates misbehave, though they are healthy themselves imaging the bladder or sphincter shows nothing. the problem is in the wiring, not the tube. cancer renal cell carcinoma (rcc), urothelial cancer, prostate cancer any part; depends on the tissue blood in the urine, or found by chance with no symptoms often nothing above it until the tumor blocks the tube. painless visible blood in the urine is cancer until proven otherwise, precisely because there is no back-pressure to warn you. the trap "burning when i pee" is felt at the outlet (station 5). the reflex is to treat it as a bladder infection (cystitis). but the same symptom comes from urethritis (the urethra), prostatitis (the prostate, next to the urethra), a low stone stuck at the uvj (where the ureter meets the bladder), or atrophic vaginitis next door. the urinalysis (ua) isn't there to confirm a uti; it tells you where to look. a clean ua in a "uti" means the bladder is probably not the problem, and you need to look elsewhere.

label: Two drawings of everything that can block the tract
text: two drawings of everything that can block the tract · these are the two most useful pictures on this page. each shows the urinary tract with every possible problem drawn in at once. study them until you can look at a presentation and say which part is at fault. that's what you'll be asked to do on call. kidney and ureter (stations 1–2): what can go wrong up high. stones in the calyx and along the ureter. a tumour in the ureter. a kink. an extra blood vessel pressing from outside. scar tissue. chronic infection. every one of them causes a swollen kidney above and an empty tube below , the typical pattern of a blocked tube. boxed labels show changes caused by the blockage. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract . bladder, control and outlet (stations 3–5): what can go wrong down low. the bladder wall has thickened from pushing against a blockage. the prostate is enlarged (bph) and has cancer. there's a pouch in the bladder wall (diverticulum), a stone, a congenital valve, a polyp, a stricture, and a tight foreskin (phimosis) at the opening. any one of these explains "can't pee" or "weak stream." your job is to work out which. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract .

label: Choosing a test: which part can it see?
text: choosing a test: which part can it see? · for the patient, this means fewer and better-chosen tests. each test shows a different part of the tract. don't choose a test from the symptom; choose it from the part you still can't see. know what each test shows, and just as important, what it misses. test what part it shows what it answers what it misses urinalysis the urine itself, not the tract is there blood, infection, protein, glucose, crystals? can't tell you where. blood on a ua could come from any part. urine culture the urine, with the organism named what organism, and what antibiotics work on it? doesn't tell you which part is infected. post-void residual how well the bladder empties does the bladder empty? doesn't tell you why it didn't empty: blockage or a weak bladder muscle. uroflow + urodynamics bladder, control gates and outlet: how they work storage pressure, voiding pressure, flow rate, sphincter coordination no anatomy. a flat flow curve says something is blocked, not where. cystoscopy bladder, control gates and outlet: a camera looks inside what does the inside of the tube actually look like? stones, tumors, strictures, prostate pushing in. only what's inside the tube. a 4 cm kidney mass is invisible. ultrasound (renal + bladder) kidney and bladder: their structure hydronephrosis, bladder volume, stones, masses bowel gas hides the ureter. depends on the operator's skill. ct urogram kidney, ureter and bladder: full structure of the upper tract stones, masses, hydronephrosis, anatomy how well it works. a widened system could be blocked now or scarred from years ago. mri pelvis bladder, control gates and outlet: soft tissue detail prostate cancer staging, pelvic floor anatomy stones (not bright on mri). acute infection. biopsy a tissue sample from where the problem is what is this growth under the microscope? sampling error. a negative biopsy rules out cancer in the cores you took, nothing more. the pattern tests get more invasive the further inside they look. a ua is cheap and only reads the urine. cystoscopy looks directly inside and is invasive. a biopsy takes tissue and can't be undone. move to a deeper test only when a simpler one hasn't told you where the problem is. when a senior asks "what's the next test?" they are really asking "which part can't you see yet?" answer that and the test picks itself.

label: Treat where the problem is, not where it hurts
text: treat where the problem is, not where it hurts · this is what separates thinking about the whole tube from just treating symptoms. the temptation is to treat where the patient is uncomfortable: at the exit. the right move is to treat where the flow first stopped.

label: BPH: the classic example
text: bph: the classic example · an enlarged prostate squeezes the urethra that runs through it (the outlet, station 5). the patient comes in with retention: the bladder can't empty, and the complaint is at the exit ("i can't go"). the bladder isn't the cause. it has been pushing against an outlet that won't open. pressure builds back up through the ureters to the kidneys, and the kidneys pay the price. a catheter fixes the exit: urine comes out. but the prostate is still there. take the catheter out and the retention comes back. the problem is at the outlet. the treatments all act there: α-blocker (tamsulosin): relaxes smooth muscle at the bladder neck and in the prostatic urethra. acts on the control gates and outlet. 5α-reductase inhibitor (finasteride): shrinks the prostate over months. acts on the gland itself. turp / holep / urolift (transurethral resection of the prostate, holmium laser enucleation of the prostate, prostatic urethral lift): remove or pull back the blocking tissue with surgery. the lasting fix at the outlet. a catheter treats the symptom. each of the above treats the cause. both are sometimes right, but you should always know which one you are doing and why.

label: The same rule for other common complaints
text: the same rule for other common complaints · presentation where the patient feels it where the problem is where you treat renal colic flank → groin (referred along the nerve's skin area, the dermatome) a stone in the ureter the ureter: let it pass, lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, stent painless gross hematuria color of urine anywhere from kidney to outlet wherever the problem is found; never the exit unless it's there urgency / frequency "i have to go" overactive bladder muscle or oversensitive bladder nerves (the bladder) the bladder: antimuscarinic, β3 agonist, behavioural changes, botulinum toxin (bont) stress incontinence leak with cough sphincter / pelvic floor (the control gates) the control gates: pelvic floor physiotherapy (pt), sling, bulking agent recurrent uti in a man dysuria something in the anatomy that lets bacteria settle: a stone, leftover urine, the prostate that underlying cause. antibiotics treat this episode; they don't fix the cause. the habit to build "stop the bleeding, stop the pain, drain the blockage" is emergency care. it buys time. it is not the fix. once the patient is stable, ask every time: where did the flow first stop, and what treats it there? then plan the lasting treatment at that spot.

label: A Worked Case — "I Can't Pee"
text: a worked case — "i can't pee" · a 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department (ed). his lower belly feels full, he hasn't urinated in 14 hours, and his last try produced "a few drops." work back up the tract. 1 the complaint at the exit · outlet "i can't pee." flow has visibly stopped at the exit. you don't yet know which part failed first. on exam the lower belly is full: the bladder can be felt, and it sounds dull when tapped above the pubic bone. he notices it at the outlet. the cause could be at the bladder or anywhere below it. the bladder isn't emptying, but you don't know why yet. decision: bladder scan before anything else. 2 find where the urine is backed up · bladder 820 ml retained. this is acute retention. the bladder can hold urine: its storing works, and is in fact overworked. pressure is building back from the outlet. the problem is either below the bladder muscle or in the nerves that sense fullness. keep looking. decision: drain the bladder (foley catheter) and keep looking for the cause at the same time. don't lose the chance to find it. 3 check the urine · ua no leukocytes, no nitrites, no blood, trace protein. a clean ua. a bladder infection (cystitis) isn't driving this. no blood, so no obvious sign of cancer yet. the simplest test has already crossed causes off the list. off the list: retention caused by a uti. 4 check the wiring · nerves (control) no back pain, no saddle anesthesia, no leg weakness, no recent neurologic change. diabetic but well-controlled, no neuropathy on exam. not on anticholinergics, decongestants, or opioids. nerve and medication causes drop off the list. cauda equina syndrome isn't the cause, but you still asked, because you'd never forgive yourself for putting in a catheter and sending home a man whose spinal cord was being squeezed. off the list: nerve-related retention, drug-induced retention. 5 focused history · bladder & outlet slow stream "for years." wakes 3× nightly. hesitancy. felt "incomplete" emptying for months. no prior catheterization, no instrumentation, no stis, no trauma. months of the outlet slowly narrowing, and now it has suddenly given out. a stricture is unlikely without past instruments or infection. this fits an enlarged prostate squeezing the urethra that runs through it. nothing is stuck inside the urethra; its wall is being squeezed from outside. working diagnosis: bph causing a long-standing outlet blockage that has now suddenly worsened. 6 feel the problem directly · digital rectal exam (dre) prostate symmetrically enlarged, smooth, rubbery, non-tender. no nodules. fits benign enlargement. no nodule means no immediate suspicion of prostate cancer on this exam. that doesn't rule it out, and a prostate-specific antigen (psa) test still belongs in the workup once the bladder is drained (acute retention itself raises psa, so timing matters). not tender, so prostatitis is off the list. off the list: acute prostatitis, prostate cancer you can feel. what the dre is feeling. an overgrown prostate (yellow) squeezing the urethra and pushing up into the bladder, which has swollen above it. the outlet is the problem. the swollen bladder is the result. burroughs wellcome co. 7 check for damage higher up · kidneys and ureters creatinine 1.4 (baseline 1.0). mild bilateral hydronephrosis. the problem is at the outlet, but back-pressure has reached the kidneys. high pressure in the bladder has pushed back through the bladder neck, the bladder and the ureters into the kidneys. this is why you don't treat retention as an exit problem and walk away. the kidneys are paying the price. draining the bladder protects the kidneys; it isn't just for comfort. what follows: recheck creatinine after draining. expect heavy urine output once the blockage is relieved (post-obstructive diuresis); watch for it. 8 problem found · outlet acute urinary retention from bph. the prostate is squeezing the urethra at the outlet. kidneys and ureters mildly affected; kidney function should recover. five stations, eight steps, one cause. notice where you stopped: you didn't need urodynamics, cystoscopy or a ct. those come next if the first treatment fails. you tested only as far as you needed to be sure enough to act. treat at the outlet. rx treatment · step by step drain now. treat the cause next. plan the lasting fix. foley catheter : relieves the back-pressure all the way up. treats the symptom. buys time. tamsulosin : relaxes the smooth muscle at the bladder neck and prostate. started right away to improve the odds of passing a voiding trial. voiding trial in 3–7 days : catheter out, to see whether the α-blocker alone lets him void. outpatient urology follow-up : psa (delayed), and a discussion of a 5α-reductase inhibitor (5-ari) vs. surgery (turp / holep / urolift). this is where the cause is actually treated. recheck kidney function : confirm the kidneys recover once the outlet is opened. the foley is not the treatment. it is the bridge to the treatment. what this case teaches the patient pointed at the exit. the bladder scan showed the bladder was swollen. the cause was the prostate at the outlet. the back-pressure had reached the kidneys. every part mattered, but only one needed the definitive treatment. ask of every patient: where did the flow first stop, and what treats it there?

label: Where it hurts vs. where the problem is: referred pain
text: where it hurts vs. where the problem is: referred pain · for the patient, this means the spot they point to is often not where the problem is. the tube is damaged in one place, but the pain is felt in the patch of skin that shares its nerve supply (the dermatome). trust the patient's pointing finger and you'll often be wrong about location. stone at the upj (where the kidney meets the ureter) → flank pain from the kidney's capsule being stretched. mimics musculoskeletal (msk) back pain. stone in the middle of the ureter → pain in the side of the abdomen. mimics appendicitis on the right, diverticulitis on the left. stone at the uvj (where the ureter meets the bladder) → groin / testicular / labial pain. mimics hernia, torsion, epididymitis. bladder problems → pain above the pubic bone, sometimes felt at the tip of the penis or in the perineum. prostatitis (the prostate, around the urethra) → perineum, low back, tip of penis, testicles, rectum. five places from one inflamed gland. kidney capsule stretch (the kidney) → flank, costovertebral angle. may spread to the shoulder on the same side if the diaphragm is irritated. the pattern: the patient's finger points to the dermatome, not the organ. it's the same lesson anywhere referred pain shows up. believe the symptom, doubt the location, and image the part you suspect.

label: The steps, in order
text: the steps, in order · work back up from where the flow stops step 1 — take the complaint at face value. → patient says "burning," "blood," "can't go," "leaking." → that names the group: storing / emptying / blood / pain. step 2 — start with the simplest test that rules out the most. → ua + culture. bladder scan if the problem is emptying. → a clean ua in a "uti" changes your path. so does a 600 ml pvr. step 3 — let the history point to the part. → nerve symptoms? → outside the tract · the nerves (control) → slow stream for years? → long-standing outlet block · prostate/urethra → painless visible blood? → assume cancer until imaged + scoped step 4 — examine the suspected part directly when you can. → dre for the prostate. look at the urethral opening (meatus). → pelvic exam where appropriate. step 5 — image the part you still can't see. → kidney or ureter? → ct urogram / renal ultrasound → how it works? → urodynamics → inside the tube? → cystoscopy step 6 — take tissue only when imaging can't answer. → biopsy is the most invasive test. use it last, and aim it. step 7 — treat where the problem is. → not where it hurts. not at the exit. not at the swelling above. → at the place where the flow first stopped.

label: Words used on this page
text: words used on this page · conduit a one-way tube. here, the whole path from kidney to outlet. station one of the five parts of the tract: kidney (1), ureter (2), bladder (3), control: sphincters, pelvic floor and nerves (4), outlet: prostate and urethra (5). lesion the spot where the tract is damaged or blocked. detrusor the muscle in the bladder wall that squeezes to empty it. sphincter a ring of muscle that holds urine in until it relaxes. hydronephrosis a kidney swollen with urine that can't drain. upj / uvj where the ureter leaves the kidney (ureteropelvic junction) and where it enters the bladder (ureterovesical junction). pvr post-void residual: urine left in the bladder after voiding. dyssynergia the bladder squeezes while the sphincter stays shut, so pressure rises with no flow. gross hematuria blood in the urine you can see. dermatome the patch of skin supplied by one spinal nerve, where referred pain is felt. may 24, 2026 · reworded october 28, 2026 — for pas, medical students, and clinical clerks the urinary tract is a one-way tube · work back up from the exit · treat where the flow first stopped ← back to reference

label: Common Consults: The ER & Inpatient Set
text: common consults: the er & inpatient set · for pa students and new learners taking first call. the emergency room (er) sees the symptom where it shows up. your job is to find where along the urinary tract the flow first broke down, and to know which consults can't wait for the workup to finish.

label: Four Steps for Every Consult
text: four steps for every consult · think through every urology consult in four steps : what the patient says → what's not working → what's physically wrong → why it happened. (these are steps of reasoning, not the five anatomical stations of the urinary tract .) each step usually falls to a different person: step examples who usually gets there 1 — what the patient says "can't pee" · "blood in urine" · "pain" · "fever" triage nurse, er attending 2 — what's not working retention (bladder won't empty). blocked flow. leaking (loss of continence). unstable blood pressure and heart rate. er physician 3 — what's physically wrong stone where the ureter enters the bladder (ureterovesical junction, uvj). enlarged prostate. clot in the bladder. testis with no blood supply. you — on consult 4 — why it happened benign prostatic hyperplasia (bph). blood thinners. bladder cancer. twisted spermatic cord. diabetes. urology, later on example: a man says "i can't pee" (step 1). his bladder is full and won't empty (step 2). his prostate is blocking the outlet (step 3). years of prostate growth plus new opioids tipped him over (step 4). the er doctor heard step 1 and worked out step 2. they called you to find step 3, the place along the urinary tract where flow first broke down , and to start planning for step 4. that is the whole consult. what "first call" actually means you are trusted to do three things, in this order. one, spot the patients who can't wait for the workup: fournier's gangrene, testicular torsion, and urosepsis with a blocked kidney. two, stabilize: drain what's swollen with trapped urine, unblock what's blocked, press on what's bleeding. three, find the problem (the station of the urinary tract that failed first) well enough that the staff urologist can plan the operation by phone. the four steps help you do these in the right order every time.

label: How to Read Each Consult Below
text: how to read each consult below · every consult below is laid out the same way. the coloured badge says how urgent it is. the line beside it says how fast it gets worse, so you know if the workup can finish before you must act. two boxes then say where the problem is and where the patient feels it, before the details start. critical
