text: example: how each card is laid out · how fast it gets worse · time until harm where the problem is the part that is actually damaged e.g. cord, fascia, ureter where the patient feels it the symptom or sign that brings them in e.g. scrotum, skin, flank then: how it looks · workup · treatment · when to call urology .

label: The Consults
text: the consults · urgent

label: 1. Urinary Retention
text: 1. urinary retention · how fast it gets worse · hours for the kidneys; minutes for the pain where the problem is the outlet, station 5 (prostate / urethra), or the nerves that control emptying (station 4) blocked outlet vs nerve problem where the patient feels it distended bladder, suprapubic pain "can't pee": the symptom, step 1 how it looks two kinds. obstructive retention : a slowly narrowed outlet (bph, urethral stricture) suddenly can't cope. something usually tips it over: alcohol, anticholinergics, decongestants, opioids, or recent surgery. history of a slow stream. big bladder, big post-void residual (pvr, urine left after voiding). neurogenic retention : think spinal cord: cauda equina, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis (ms) flare, diabetic autonomic neuropathy. look for saddle numbness, leg weakness, bowel changes, recent back pain. acute on chronic is the most common er picture: a man with years of lower urinary tract symptoms (luts) who suddenly can't void after a hip replacement and a few opioids. workup bladder scan first. over 300 ml (local thresholds vary) in a patient who can't void is retention. drain with a foley catheter before you finish the workup. urinalysis (ua) + basic metabolic panel (bmp). renal ultrasound if you suspect both kidneys are swollen (bilateral hydronephrosis) or creatinine is up. always ask the nerve questions out loud: saddle numbness, legs, bowel, back pain. if any are positive, order an mri of the lumbar spine stat, not a urology consult. treatment the foley drains the bladder (station 3) and takes back-pressure off the ureters (station 2). start tamsulosin right away if the outlet is blocked; it makes the later trial without a catheter more likely to work. watch for post-obstructive diuresis, a surge of urine once the blockage is relieved (urine output >200 ml/hr for 2 consecutive hours, or >3 l in 24 hours, after decompression): replace half of each hour's output with iv fluids, recheck electrolytes. trial of void in 3–7 days as an outpatient if stable. when to call urology can't pass the catheter: call before forcing it. a false passage (a new tear off the urethra) in a man with bph or stricture costs weeks. visible blood in the urine with retention: likely clots blocking the bladder (clot retention); needs a 3-way catheter for irrigation, see below. retention with sepsis or acute kidney injury (aki): admit, call now. any suspicion of a spinal cord problem: neurosurgery first, urology second. urgent

label: 2. Renal Colic / Ureteric Stone
text: 2. renal colic / ureteric stone · how fast it gets worse · hours if infected; days if not where the problem is the ureter, station 2: where it leaves the kidney (upj), crosses the pelvic brim, or enters the bladder (uvj) its three natural narrow points where the patient feels it flank → groin → testis/labia pain moves lower along the same nerve's skin area as the stone moves down how it looks sudden, severe pain that comes in waves (colic). the patient can't find a comfortable position, unlike peritonitis, where they lie still. blood seen only on testing (microscopic hematuria) is common; visible (gross) hematuria is possible. nausea and vomiting are prominent. pain moving toward the groin or scrotum suggests the stone has moved down to the uvj. workup non-contrast ct of the kidneys, ureters and bladder (ct kub) is the test. it shows the stone, any swelling of the kidney (hydronephrosis), and other causes (abdominal aortic aneurysm, appendicitis). ua looking for blood and infection. complete blood count (cbc) + bmp. if pregnant: ultrasound first, then mri if needed; ct is the last resort. see stones in pregnancy for the trimester-by-trimester plan. treatment stones <5 mm in the lower (distal) ureter: ~80% pass. nsaids (ketorolac if kidney function is ok), an anti-nausea drug, strain the urine, outpatient follow-up. stones 5–10 mm: mixed. about half pass with time. tamsulosin (medical expulsive therapy, met) is debated but standard for distal stones over 5 mm. outpatient urology in 1–2 weeks if uncomplicated. stones >10 mm: rarely pass on their own. plan a procedure (ureteroscopy / shock wave lithotripsy). when to call urology infected, blocked kidney : fever + stone + hydronephrosis. treat as urosepsis until proven otherwise. drain it now, see below. only one kidney, and it is blocked. both sides blocked. aki from the blockage. pain that won't settle despite good pain relief. stone >10 mm: for planned treatment later, not in the emergency department (ed). urgent

label: 3. Gross Hematuria
text: 3. gross hematuria · how fast it gets worse · hours if clot retention; days if not where the problem is anywhere from the kidney (station 1) to the urethral opening (meatus) finding which one is the whole job where the patient feels it color of the urine: the symptom, step 1 tells you nothing about where the bleeding starts how it looks ask when in the stream the blood appears; there are three patterns. initial hematuria (blood at the start, then clearing) → urethra. terminal hematuria (clear, then blood at the end) → bladder neck / trigone (base of the bladder). total hematuria (blood throughout) → bladder or upper tract (kidney, ureter). painless visible blood in an adult's urine is cancer until proven otherwise. painful visible blood is usually a stone or infection. blood thinners don't cause hematuria by themselves; they reveal a problem that was already there. work it up the same way either way. workup ua + culture (rule out infection first; if positive, treat it, then reassess). cbc, bmp, clotting tests (coags). ct urogram for the kidneys, ureters and bladder. cystoscopy (a camera into the bladder) to see the bladder lining: flexible, in clinic, the gold standard for finding bladder cancer. check for clot retention at the bedside: feel above the pubic bone, bladder scan if unsure. treatment if no clot retention and stable: outpatient workup. if clots are blocking the bladder: 3-way foley (22–24 french (fr), large bore) with continuous bladder irrigation (cbi). wash out the clots by hand with a toomey syringe before starting cbi; running cbi into a bladder full of clot just blows it up. reverse blood thinners if the bleeding is significant. type and screen; transfuse for anemia that causes symptoms. when to call urology clot retention requiring cbi. clots that won't clear after washout by hand and cbi. unstable vital signs: bleeding from anywhere in the genitourinary (gu) tract that drops the blood pressure means call now. recent urologic procedure with new bleeding: assume it's from the procedure; see the post-op section. any visible hematuria needs outpatient urology follow-up. write this clearly in the discharge plan; don't assume the patient will find their own way to clinic. critical

label: 4. Urosepsis
text: 4. urosepsis · how fast it gets worse · hours; risk of death rises with each one where the problem is the kidney and ureter (stations 1–2): blocked and infected a closed space full of bacteria where the patient feels it fever, fast heart rate, low blood pressure whole-body signs: the symptom (step 1) at its worst how it looks fever + flank pain + hydronephrosis = kidney infection behind a blockage (obstructed pyelonephritis) until proven otherwise. at-risk groups: diabetic, immunosuppressed, elderly, a recent scope or catheter, or a known stone. they can look surprisingly well one hour and crash the next. an infected, blocked kidney is an infection in a closed space. antibiotics alone won't drain it. the pressure has to come off. what a blocked, infected kidney looks like inside. pus fills the collecting system; abscesses are scattered through the outer kidney (cortex); the kidney tissue is inflamed. drainage is not optional. antibiotics arrive through the bloodstream; they don't get into the closed, blocked space. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract . workup lactate, blood cultures, ua + urine culture, cbc, bmp, coags. ct abdomen/pelvis with contrast (or non-contrast if aki) to find the blockage. sepsis bundle: fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, control of the source. don't wait for cultures to start antibiotics, but know that antibiotics are the second step, not the first. treatment antibiotics won't work until it's drained. two options: ureteral stent : placed by urology from below (retrograde), in the operating room (or). faster if available. percutaneous nephrostomy : a tube through the back into the kidney, placed by interventional radiology (ir), at the bedside or in the ir suite. often the right call after hours. the choice depends on your hospital: whoever can drain it faster. both work. the wrong answer is "let's see if the antibiotics work." when to call urology always, right away, at the same time as calling ir. if the picture is clear enough, this is the consult where you call before the ct result is back. expect icu admission. critical

label: 5. Fournier's Gangrene
text: 5. fournier's gangrene · how fast it gets worse · only the time to the or matters where the problem is the tissue layers (fascia) of the perineum: a layers problem, not a urinary tract one flesh-eating (necrotizing) infection spreading along colles' / buck's / dartos fascia where the patient feels it scrotal / perineal skin often looks deceptively mild early if you suspect fournier's, stop reading and call. pain much worse than the exam in the perineum, scrotum or groin, especially in a diabetic, obese or immunosuppressed patient, is fournier's until proven otherwise. the skin changes show up hours after the deeper tissue starts dying. crepitus (crackling gas under the skin) is late. unstable vital signs come later still. how fast the patient gets to surgery to cut away dead tissue (debridement) is the one factor linked to survival. imaging delays the or. antibiotics don't reach dead tissue. cut. how it looks who gets it: diabetic, immunosuppressed, heavy alcohol use, an abscess near the rectum, a recent perineal procedure, or a long-term catheter. severe pain in the perineum or scrotum. early on, the skin can look like cellulitis (pink, warm, swollen), then turns dusky, purple, blistered, and finally black. crepitus is very specific but often absent. foul-smelling, "dishwater" pus if the skin is open. sicker than the skin suggests. workup this is a bedside diagnosis. if you are sure, ct is a delay you can't afford. if you're unsure and the patient is stable, ct can show gas in the tissue layers and how far it has spread, but a normal ct doesn't rule it out. the lrinec score (a lab-based risk score for necrotizing fasciitis) supports the diagnosis but can't make it. draw labs (cbc, bmp, lactate, crp, glucose, coags) on the way to the or. treatment broad-spectrum antibiotics that also cover anaerobes (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + vancomycin, per local protocol). start in the ed. aggressive fluids and support (resuscitation). admit to icu. surgery to cut away dead tissue. debridement is the treatment. everything else is support. expect repeat trips to the or every 24–48 hours until clean. a suprapubic catheter (through the lower belly into the bladder) or a diverting colostomy may be needed, depending on how far it spreads. when to call urology now. before any of the above. call urology and general surgery together: the debridement often crosses into both their areas. critical

label: 6. Priapism
text: 6. priapism · how fast it gets worse · act within 4 h to save function; 24 h is too late where the problem is the erectile chambers (corpora cavernosa): blood can't drain out (ischemic) or a leaking artery (arterial fistula) in non-ischemic where the patient feels it painful, rigid penis >4 hours tip (glans) usually soft, shaft (corpora) rigid how it looks two types, totally different problems. ischemic (low-flow, veno-occlusive) : blood is trapped, so it acts like a compartment syndrome of the erectile chambers. painful, fully rigid, dark blood when you draw it out (aspiration). causes: sickle cell, leukemia, injections into the penis (intracavernosal), pde5 inhibitors, trazodone, cocaine. treat as an emergency. non-ischemic (high-flow, arterial) follows perineal trauma. partly rigid, painless, bright red blood on aspiration. not an emergency: managed on a planned basis by blocking the artery (selective embolization). workup history (sickle cell? trauma? drugs?). a blood gas from the erectile chamber (cavernosal blood gas) tells them apart: dark and acidotic = ischemic; bright and like arterial blood = non-ischemic. doppler ultrasound confirms it if unsure. treatment — ischemic aspirate the erectile chamber (corpus cavernosum) with a 16–18g angiocatheter or butterfly needle through the glans or side of the shaft. remove the dark blood. irrigate with saline. inject phenylephrine: dilute in saline (100–500 mcg/ml); give ~200 mcg every 3–5 minutes, watching blood pressure (bp) and heart rate (hr). maximum 1 mg within 1 hour. if aspiration + phenylephrine fail: surgical shunt, however long it has lasted. ischemia >48 hours → discuss an early penile prosthesis. the risk of permanent erectile dysfunction rises with every hour after the 4-hour mark. treatment — non-ischemic watch and wait at first. many settle on their own. if it persists, block the leaking branch of the pudendal artery (selective embolization). not a same-day procedure. when to call urology for any priapism >4 hours, call. if it's ischemic, you want urology at the bedside for the aspiration and injection. if it's non-ischemic, you still want them planning the embolization with ir. critical

label: 7. Testicular Torsion
text: 7. testicular torsion · how fast it gets worse · 6 h to save the testis where the problem is the spermatic cord: blood supply cut off (a network problem: the testicular artery) the twist chokes the testicular artery where the patient feels it acute scrotal pain often spreading to the lower abdomen how it looks teen or young adult, sudden severe scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting. sometimes wakes them from sleep. the testis sits high and lies sideways (transverse lie); the cremasteric reflex is absent. lifting the testis doesn't ease the pain (prehn's sign negative). in epididymitis lifting helps, but don't base the diagnosis on prehn's sign alone. it can look atypical in younger children and adult men. never bet against torsion when scrotal pain starts suddenly. workup a bedside diagnosis. doppler ultrasound shows reduced or absent blood flow to the testis, but don't delay surgery for an ultrasound if the picture is convincing. the clock starts when the cord twists, not when the patient arrives. treatment to the or now: open the scrotum, untwist the cord, and fix both testes in place (bilateral orchiopexy). you can try untwisting by hand in the ed ("opening the book": rotate the affected testis outward, away from the midline) while the or gets ready. it eases pain and may restore flow, but it doesn't replace the operation. both sides are fixed because the other side has the same built-in weakness (bell-clapper deformity). when to call urology as soon as you suspect it. nothing by mouth (npo); book the patient for the or. the testis is saved in >90% at <6 hours, <10% at >24 hours. the consult is not "rule out torsion"; it's "this is torsion until urology rules it out in the or." urgent

label: 8. Traumatic GU Injury
text: 8. traumatic gu injury · how fast it gets worse · depends on the injury where the problem is any station, kidney (1) to outlet (5), depending on how the injury happened the direction of force predicts what's hurt where the patient feels it blood in the urine, perineal bruising, blood at the urethral opening small surface signs, big underlying injury renal trauma blunt: usually a motor vehicle collision, sports impact or fall. penetrating: gunshot or stab. the amount of blood in the urine does not match how bad the injury is; a major injury to the kidney's main vessels (renal pedicle) can cause very little. ct abdomen/pelvis with iv contrast (with a delayed phase to see the collecting system) grades the injury (aast trauma grades i–v). most blunt low-grade injuries (i–iii) are managed without surgery. contrast actively leaking (extravasation) or unstable vital signs → angio-embolization or or. watch for late bleeding from a pseudoaneurysm; keep a low threshold to readmit. bladder trauma pelvic fracture + visible hematuria = bladder injury until proven otherwise. ct cystogram (fill the bladder with contrast through a catheter, then scan) is the test, not a contrast ct alone, which can miss a rupture because the bladder isn't filled under pressure. two patterns: extraperitoneal (leaks outside the abdominal cavity; most common, with pelvic fracture): foley drainage 10–14 days, repeat cystogram before the catheter comes out. intraperitoneal (leaks into the abdominal cavity; blunt trauma to a full bladder, classically a seatbelt injury): surgical repair. always. urethral trauma blood at the meatus is a stop sign. don't place a foley until a urethral injury is ruled out. two patterns: posterior (pelvic fracture; a "high-riding prostate" on digital rectal exam (dre), though that finding is unreliable) → retrograde urethrogram (rug); often managed with a suprapubic catheter and repair later. anterior (straddle injury) → rug; may be repaired right away or stented, depending on the injury. when to call urology any blood at the meatus before catheterization. visible hematuria in a trauma patient. pelvic fracture with any gu sign. penetrating gu trauma: assume it needs surgery until proven otherwise. renal injury aast grade iii or higher. urgent

label: 9. Post-Operative Complications
text: 9. post-operative complications · how fast it gets worse · varies; take any new finding seriously where the problem is whichever station was operated on prostate, kidney, bladder, ureter where the patient feels it drain output, urine color, fever, stalled bowel (ileus) each of which can mean several things bleeding after turp (transurethral resection of the prostate) some bleeding is expected: pink urine, small clots, clearing over 24–48 hours. bright red, heavy, or with clots the cbi can't keep up with is not expected. turn up the irrigation, wash out clots by hand, check coags, and check the catheter balloon hasn't been pulled into the space where the prostate was (prostatic fossa), pressing in the wrong place. bleeding that persists → back to the or to cauterize (fulguration). urine leak after partial nephrectomy or pyeloplasty high drain output that smells like urine, or drain fluid creatinine much higher than blood (serum) creatinine, confirms a urine leak. most heal with longer drainage and a ureteral stent to lower the pressure inside the kidney, so the leak can seal. a leak that persists → percutaneous nephrostomy + stent. reoperation is rare. catheter pulled or fell out after prostatectomy or urethroplasty don't blindly put it back. call urology. a catheter pushed through a fresh join (anastomosis) can tear it open. it often needs placing with a cystoscope over a wire. treat this as a same-night call. no urine after cystectomy with ileal conduit stoma not draining. first: is the stoma alive (pink)? a dusky stoma means its blood supply is failing: an emergency. then check the catheters in the conduit; a mucus plug is the usual cause. flush the conduit catheters gently. if still no output, image the join between ureters and bowel (ureteroenteric anastomosis). ileus + fever + high white count after pelvic urologic surgery think urine collection (urinoma), abscess, ureter injury. ct abdomen/pelvis with delayed images. the picture you don't want to miss is "a leaking join disguised as ileus." when to call urology any unexpected finding in the first 30 days after a urologic operation goes to the surgeon who operated, not just to whoever is on for urology. that surgeon knows what they built and what should and shouldn't be happening.

label: The Triage Matrix
text: the triage matrix · the rule: how fast the problem gets worse decides how fast you move. if it will do harm before your workup can finish, act first and confirm later. if it's slower than that, image and plan. critical · act now fournier's gangrene — straight to the or testicular torsion — 6 h to save the testis urosepsis with obstruction — drain first ischemic priapism — harm after 4 h penetrating gu trauma unstable vital signs from any gu cause gets worse faster than the workup urgent · stabilize, then find the cause acute retention — drain, then plan colic with fever — check it isn't blocked gross hematuria with clot retention pyelonephritis without obstruction blunt renal trauma grade iii+ post-op complications within 30 days act this shift not urgent · plan where they go stable ureteric stone <5 mm, no fever, no aki asymptomatic microscopic hematuria chronic retention , stable creatinine, no overflow uncomplicated cystitis non-ischemic priapism (rare to see at all) stable grade i–ii renal trauma outpatient or routine the one question for every consult, ask: will this do harm before my workup is finished? if yes → act now, confirm later. if no → confirm, then act. this one habit separates a useful first call from one that holds up the operation.

label: When to Wake Up the Urologist
text: when to wake up the urologist · on first call you need rules, not judgment calls. use these. they deliberately lean toward waking someone up. wake them up. right now. suspected fournier's gangrene . no imaging needed. suspected testicular torsion while the testis can still be saved. obstructed pyelonephritis : fever + hydronephrosis + signs of sepsis. ischemic priapism >4 hours. gu bleeding with unstable vital signs . penetrating gu trauma. can't place a catheter in acute retention with rising creatinine or sepsis . any post-operative urology patient within 30 days with a new acute finding. call within the shift, not at 0300. foley placed for retention, patient stable, no aki. a call at handover is fine. renal colic, controlled pain, no fever, no aki, stone likely to pass. visible hematuria, no clot retention, stable hemoglobin, blood thinners reviewed. stable grade i–ii renal trauma. uncomplicated urinary tract infection (uti) in an otherwise healthy patient. handle yourself; pass to clinic. asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with a clean ua and no risk factors: work up as an outpatient. stable chronic retention without overflow incontinence or aki. phimosis (tight foreskin) without blockage. painless scrotal masses (document them and arrange follow-up). the default when in doubt, call. the cost of an unnecessary call is one annoyed urologist. the cost of a missed fournier's or torsion is a patient who loses tissue or dies. the two risks are not close. you will lose nothing in the long run by being the pa who called at 0300 about a possible torsion that turned out to be epididymitis. you will lose a lot by being the one who didn't.

label: A Worked Consult
text: a worked consult · post-op day 1 (pod1) after a right total hip replacement (tha). 68-year-old man. hasn't voided since the foley came out 6 hours ago. the er is involved because the floor team is unsure. the call comes to you. 1 what the er / floor sees · step 1: what the patient says "post-op patient can't void." the floor team has the complaint and a routine post-op picture. vitals normal so far. they want to know if they can put the catheter back, or whether something else is going on. the floor's instinct is to put the foley back in. yours should be to find the problem before you put anything in. 2 what you check first · step 2: what's not working bladder scan. vitals. med list. scan: 720 ml. that confirms retention: the bladder really is full, not just feeling full. vitals: hr 88, bp 138/82, afebrile. no sepsis. medications since the or: spinal anesthetic, fentanyl by patient-controlled pump (pca), ketorolac, ondansetron, oxybutynin (someone ordered it for "bladder spasms" before surgery and it was never stopped). the pca and oxybutynin are the immediate reason the bladder won't empty. underneath them may sit chronic bph. working idea: acute retention brought on by drugs, almost certainly on top of long-standing luts. 3 targeted history · step 3: what's physically wrong "have you had trouble peeing before this?" yes. slow stream for two years. nocturia twice a night. has been "meaning to see somebody about my prostate." never had retention before. no back pain, no leg weakness, no saddle anesthesia, no bowel change. no previous catheters or scopes. this is long-standing outlet blockage tipped into acute retention by an anticholinergic + opioids + lying flat, with the underlying problem at the outlet (station 5: the prostate). off the list: spinal cord problem. on the list: bph, now showing itself. 4 drain the bladder · relieve back-pressure foley, 16 fr, sterile, single attempt. passes without difficulty. 780 ml out over the first 15 minutes. no gross hematuria. patient comfortable right away. the catheter has bought you time to work things out; don't waste it. order: bmp, ua, urine culture (it'll grow eventually if anything; better to know now). confirm afebrile, watch for the next hour. result: creatinine 1.1 (baseline 1.0). ua clean. no infection. no aki worth a consult on its own. 5 what urology needs to know · step 4: why it happened the 30-second handoff. when you call the staff urologist or the resident, give them this, in this order: "68 y/o man, pod1 right tha, acute retention 720 ml on scan." "two-year history of luts, never retained before. no neuro symptoms." "foley passed easily, drained 780 ml, no hematuria." "bmp normal, ua clean, afebrile." "on pca and oxybutynin — i'd like to stop the oxybutynin and start tamsulosin." "plan: leave foley for 48–72 hours, trial of void after offending meds are off, urology clinic follow-up." that is the whole consult. you found where the problem is, drained it, named the root cause, and offered a plan. the urologist either agrees and goes back to sleep, or changes one thing. either way you have done your job. 6 management · the outlet (station 5: prostate and urethra) foley + tamsulosin + stop the offenders. discontinue oxybutynin. step the pca down to an as-needed (prn) oral opioid plus regular acetaminophen. start tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly. foley to a leg bag; teach the patient and family how to care for it. document: "acute urinary retention post-arthroplasty, multifactorial — anticholinergic, opioid, supine state — on a background of clinical bph. decompressed. trial of void (tov) planned in 48–72 hours after offending agents discontinued. outpatient urology referral placed." 7 what decides where he goes · what you are watching for the trial of void decides everything. trial of void in 48–72 hours. three outcomes, three plans: voids well, low pvr (<150 ml) → home on tamsulosin, outpatient urology in 4–6 weeks. discharged when ortho clears him. voids partially, pvr 150–400 ml → use judgment. often replace catheter, try again in a week as outpatient. tamsulosin continued. fails to void, or pvr >400 ml → foley with leg bag home, outpatient urology in 1–2 weeks, honest conversation about bph workup and likely intervention (medical vs surgical). the hospital stay is no longer about urology: orthopedics decides when he goes home, based on the hip. urology's contribution is the bladder plan that travels home with him. what this consult teaches you did not need urodynamics. you did not need cystoscopy. you did not need to wake anyone up. you found what's physically wrong (the prostate, at the outlet, station 5), found the trigger (drugs acting on bladder control, station 4), relieved what wasn't working (retention, step 2), and handed off a plan that holds up after discharge. most of your consults will look like this. the point of all the other entries in this document is so that you recognize the ones that don't — and call accordingly. written may 24, 2026 — for a pa student taking first call the four steps first, so the cases make sense when they arrive. from where the patient feels it to where the problem is. ← back to reference

label: Procedures the Trainee Will Do
text: procedures the trainee will do · the bedside set for pas, medical students, and clinical clerks. foley, suprapubic tap, urine collection, bladder irrigation, stoma check. step by step, with what goes wrong attached — because when it goes wrong is when you'll need to think, not when you're following the steps.

label: Three Ways a Procedure Goes Wrong
text: three ways a procedure goes wrong · every procedure below can go wrong in three ways you need to recognize: it didn't work, it was the wrong procedure (right steps, wrong reason), or it worked but the result tells you something you didn't expect to hear. the steps are the easy part. knowing what goes wrong is why you read this twice. before you do anything sterile confirm: right patient, right side, right indication, allergies (especially latex and chlorhexidine), anticoagulation status, mental capacity to consent. document the indication in the chart before you do the procedure, not after. "i did a foley because the patient was retaining 800 ml on scan after failing to void for 8 hours" is a different note from "foley placed per request." 1

label: Foley Catheter Placement
text: foley catheter placement · urethra → bladder (stations 5 → 3) · sterile indication acute urinary retention (decompression). accurate output monitoring in a critically ill patient. healing of a urinary tract injury or fresh anastomosis. procedural — perioperative drainage where prolonged surgery is expected. contraindication / call before you try blood at the meatus in a trauma patient. stop. get a retrograde urethrogram. suspected urethral disruption (pelvic fracture, blood at the meatus; a high-riding prostate is classic but unreliable). recent urethral reconstruction or fresh anastomosis — call the operating surgeon. known stricture disease that has previously required cystoscopic guidance. kit (16 fr is the default for men and women) 16 fr 2-way foley (coudé tip — see below — for the difficult male). sterile gloves, drapes, prep solution, 10 ml syringe of sterile water, lubricant (lidocaine jelly preferred for men), drainage bag. bladder scanner, ideally, before and after. standard technique — male position supine, expose. prep with the dominant hand contaminated as soon as you hold the penis — use the other hand for the catheter. hold the penis perpendicular to the body. instill 10 ml of lidocaine jelly into the urethra , hold meatus closed for 2 minutes — this is not optional, it relaxes the external sphincter and patients tolerate the catheter without it badly. advance the catheter steadily to the hub. most resistance is at the membranous urethra (external sphincter) — ask the patient to take a slow breath in, sphincter relaxes. confirm urine return before inflating. if no urine returns and you have not reached the hub, do not inflate. inflate the balloon with 10 ml sterile water. gently retract until the balloon meets the bladder neck. standard technique — female position supine, knees flexed, frog-legged. identify the urethral meatus — between the clitoris and vaginal introitus. in post-menopausal or obese patients it can be retracted; use the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand to spread the labia and visualize. prep, lubricate, advance until urine returns or to the hub. if the catheter goes into the vagina, leave it there as a marker and pass a second catheter above it into the urethra. then remove the misplaced one. what goes wrong no urine on initial pass. if the bladder scan was >200 ml, the catheter is in a false passage or coiled. do not inflate. withdraw, irrigate the catheter to confirm patency, retry with more lube and more time. hematuria during passage. stop. means you've created a false passage or scraped a stricture. call urology. resistance at the prostate. the most common stopping point in older men. see the decision tree below. balloon won't inflate. catheter is in the urethra, not the bladder. do not force. withdraw and reposition. patient in severe pain mid-procedure. stop. reassess. often a stricture or false passage. the difficult male catheterization — decision tree 1. standard 16 fr fails at the prostate. → try a coudé tip 16 fr coudé. the curved tip points up (toward the patient's belly) — keep the indicator stripe pointing at 12 o'clock during advancement. this rides over the median lobe of the prostate. most bph-related failures end here. 2. coudé fails. → upsize, don't downsize counterintuitive. a larger catheter (18 or 20 fr) is stiffer and rides over the prostate more reliably than a 14 fr, which kinks. downsizing is for strictures, not bph. if you cannot tell stricture from bph, stop and call. 3. two passes have failed, or there is fresh blood. → stop. call urology. the pa's rule: two failed attempts is the ceiling. a third attempt creates more false passages and more bleeding. urology will place over a wire under cystoscopic guidance. that preserves the urethra for future catheterizations. a third blind attempt does not. 4. the bladder is dangerously full and urology cannot come immediately. → percutaneous suprapubic tap as a bridge see procedure #2. decompresses the bladder while urology mobilizes. not a definitive solution. document the bridge clearly. removal deflate the balloon by drawing back with the syringe — do not cut the inflation port. withdraw gently. if you meet resistance on deflation, the balloon may not have fully decompressed (check by attempting to overinflate, then deflate again). persistent failure to deflate is a call to urology, not a yank. 2

label: Suprapubic Bladder Aspiration / Percutaneous Decompression
text: suprapubic bladder aspiration / percutaneous decompression · abdominal wall → bladder (station 3) · sterile indication urgent decompression when urethral catheterization has failed and urology is delayed. sterile urine sample in an infant or non-cooperative patient where catheter sample is impractical (less common in adults). contraindication empty or unidentifiable bladder on scan — confirm volume first. coagulopathy, anticoagulation — relative; weigh against retention severity. prior lower abdominal surgery with possible adherent bowel. suprapubic skin infection at the insertion site. technique (single-stick decompression) confirm bladder volume on scan (≥300 ml ideal — gives you a target). identify insertion: 2 fingerbreadths above the symphysis pubis, midline. prep, drape, local anesthetic with lidocaine through the planned tract. advance an 18g spinal needle perpendicular to the skin, aspirating as you go. urine return confirms intravesical position. for sample only: collect, withdraw, dress. for decompression bridge: use a dedicated suprapubic catheter kit per institutional protocol. what goes wrong no urine return. either the bladder is not where you thought (re-scan) or you are too superficial. do not redirect blindly; reconfirm landmarks. frank blood return. withdraw. likely vessel rather than bladder; rescan and reposition. stool / cloudy non-urine fluid. bowel injury until proven otherwise. withdraw, broad-spectrum antibiotics, call surgery. the decompression that isn't yours alone a formal indwelling suprapubic catheter — not just an aspiration — is a urologic procedure. the single-stick aspiration described above is a temporizing maneuver, used when a patient is in distress and an indwelling solution is minutes away. place an aspiration; arrange an indwelling tube. document the gap explicitly. 3

label: Urine Collection for Culture
text: urine collection for culture · urethra (station 5) / the urine itself · a clean sample is everything why the technique matters a poorly collected sample is worse than no sample. it generates a false positive — bacteria from the perineum colonize the cup — and you end up treating a culture, not a patient. the most common urology error on the consult service is treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in a contaminated specimen. methods, in order of cleanliness method clean enough for caveat clean-catch midstream symptomatic outpatient women, men with intact prepuce coach the technique — most failures are technique failures, not biology. straight catheter sample hospitalized patients, anyone who cannot midstream one-time pass. discard the first 5 ml (urethral flora). collect from the stream. catheter port aspiration patients with indwelling foley sample from the port, not the bag . bag urine is colonized within hours regardless of patient. suprapubic aspiration definitive — used clinically rarely in adults the gold standard. any growth is real. how to read what comes back >10⁵ cfu/ml of a single organism with pyuria + symptoms → uti, treat. >10⁵ cfu/ml, no pyuria, no symptoms → asymptomatic bacteriuria. do not treat outside of pregnancy and pre-urologic-instrumentation cases. treating it selects resistance and changes nothing. mixed flora, two or three organisms → contaminated sample. recollect with better technique before deciding anything. pyuria with no growth → think atypicals, prior antibiotic, urolithiasis with inflammation, tuberculosis if subacute, or interstitial cystitis. the teaching point a urine culture is a question, not an answer. the answer comes from matching the culture to the patient . bacteria in a cup with no fever, no dysuria, no flank pain is colonization. bacteria in a cup with sepsis is urosepsis. same lab result. different diseases. 4

label: Continuous Bladder Irrigation (CBI) Setup
text: continuous bladder irrigation (cbi) setup · bladder (station 3) · clot management indication gross hematuria with clot retention. post-turp / post-prostatectomy / post-cystoscopy with significant bleeding. prevention of clot formation in expected bleeding (immediately post-turp). kit 3-way foley — 22 or 24 fr. the third lumen is the inflow channel. a 3-way foley is non-negotiable; you cannot run cbi through a 2-way. sterile saline irrigation bags (3 l) ×2 minimum, with y-tubing. drainage bag — large capacity, urometer if monitoring closely. toomey or piston syringe, 60 ml, sterile saline for manual evacuation. setup, in order manual clot evacuation first. disconnect the drainage tubing. use a toomey syringe with sterile saline. inject 60 ml, withdraw, repeat until the return is pink, not red. you cannot irrigate continuously through a bladder full of clot — the fluid pools above the clot and the bladder distends without flow. hang the irrigation bag, prime the inflow line. connect inflow to the third port of the foley. connect outflow to the drainage bag. start irrigation at a rate that keeps the effluent pink, not red . titrate up if the effluent darkens; titrate down once clear. track input and output meticulously. net output should exceed net input — this is your reassurance that flow is forward. what goes wrong bladder distends, no outflow. clot has occluded the eyelets of the catheter. stop the inflow. manually evacuate clots. restart only when patency is confirmed. bright red effluent persists or worsens. bleeding is outpacing your irrigation. increase rate, manually evacuate again, check coags, call urology. patient with abdominal pain and tense suprapubic fullness on cbi. distension. stop the irrigation immediately. assume clot occlusion until proven otherwise. you can rupture a bladder this way. negative net output (more in than out over the shift). stop, evacuate, re-set. document. the cbi rule cbi is not a substitute for clot evacuation; it is a maintenance system after the bladder is clear. starting cbi on top of a clot-filled bladder makes things worse. evacuate, then irrigate. 5

label: Urostomy / Ileal Conduit Stoma Assessment
text: urostomy / ileal conduit stoma assessment · bladder substitute (station 3) · blood-supply check what you're assessing for stoma viability — is the bowel mucosa pink and healthy? output — volume, character, presence of mucus (expected) versus frank blood or pus (not). skin around the stoma — appropriate fit of the appliance, no leakage, no excoriation. patency — anuria from a conduit is a workup, not a wait. the 30-second exam color. healthy stoma is beefy pink to red. pale pink is okay. dusky purple is ischemia. black is necrosis. both are calls now. moisture. mucosa should look glistening. dry, dull, or shriveled is a problem. edema. some swelling for the first 6 weeks post-op is normal. increasing edema later is not. retraction or prolapse. stoma flush or below skin level after maturation is retraction. stoma protruding several cm is prolapse. both prompt urology review, neither is usually emergent. output. a healthy adult ileal conduit produces 1–2 l/day of urine with mucus strands. no output in 4–6 hours, with the stoma viable, is a workup — irrigate the conduit catheters gently with saline (mucus plug is common) and call if no return. what goes wrong dusky stoma. vascular emergency. operating team needs to know within minutes. do not wait for "it might pink up." no output, viable stoma. irrigate gently. if still nothing, image (ct) to assess the ureteroenteric anastomosis and the conduit lumen. frank blood from the stoma. either intraluminal (bleeding from inside the conduit or upstream) or extrinsic (skin trauma from the appliance). inspect; if intraluminal, call. skin breakdown around the stoma. appliance fit problem. the wound ostomy nurse is your friend; this is in their territory. the mental model for ileal conduit an ileal conduit is a short segment of small bowel that has been disconnected from the gi tract and reconnected to the ureters at one end, with the other end brought out as a stoma. it is not a bladder. it does not store. it passively drains. urine has bowel mucus in it (normal) and is mildly more acidic and salty than ordinary urine. anuria in a conduit patient is a mechanical problem until proven otherwise — mucus plug, kinked appliance, anastomotic issue — not a renal problem.

label: The Common Thread
text: the common thread · each procedure above has the same shape: a defined indication, an absolute contraindication, a sequence of steps, and a point where it goes wrong and is no longer yours to fix. the expert is not the person who never fails — it is the person who recognizes the failure two steps earlier than the novice and stops. three rules that survive every procedure two failed attempts is the ceiling. any procedure. the third attempt creates the complication that becomes the consult. if you cannot name what's going wrong, you do not understand the procedure well enough to continue. stop. reread. restart or escalate. document the indication before, not after. if the procedure goes wrong, the note that says "placed because creatinine rising on retention of 800 ml" reads very differently from "placed per order." written may 24, 2026 — for pas, medical students, and clinical clerks ← back to reference

label: Medications & Their Stations
text: medications & their stations · every urology drug works on one part of the urinary tract, through one kind of receptor. learn which part and which receptor, and the rest follows. memorize the drug without knowing how it works and you'll pick the wrong one for the right problem.

label: The Map
text: the map · the five stations of the urinary tract, from the kidney that makes urine to the urethra that lets it out (see the urinary tract ), four drug classes that matter for holding and emptying urine, and two extras that show up all the time. here is where each one works: kidney filtration, concentration 1 antibiotics (concentration matters), desmopressin (concentrating) where the urine is made; where some antibiotics achieve their working concentration. ureter smooth muscle, peristalsis 2 α1-blockers (met, medical expulsive therapy: drugs to help a stone pass) relaxation of distal ureter facilitates stone passage. bladder (detrusor) m3 (contract), β3 (relax) 3 antimuscarinics, β3 agonists, bont (botulinum toxin) injected into the bladder overactive bladder — quiet the detrusor or relax it. bladder neck / internal sphincter α1a-rich 4 α1-blockers (bph, benign prostatic hyperplasia: symptoms, voiding trial) open the smooth-muscle gate to allow flow. urethra / prostate α1a smooth muscle + glandular tissue 5 α1-blockers (dynamic), 5α-reductase inhibitors (static), pde5 the two components of bph: smooth-muscle tone and gland volume — two drug classes, two targets. the cargo · urine itself not a station — what flows through the conduit c phenazopyridine (urinary analgesic) numbs the symptom in the cargo. treats nothing. useful, and dangerous when mistaken for definitive therapy. the three questions when you see a urology medication on a chart, ask three questions. where is the problem? where does this drug work? do those match? tamsulosin for retention from bph: problem at the prostate (station 5), drug works at the bladder neck and prostate (stations 4–5), match. oxybutynin for retention from bph: problem at the prostate (station 5), drug works on the bladder (station 3) — the drug will quiet the bladder that's already failing to empty. mismatch. you just made it worse.

label: The Drug Classes
text: the drug classes · s 4·5·2

label: α1-Adrenergic Blockers
text: α1-adrenergic blockers · α1a (prostate, bladder neck) · α1b (vasculature) · α1d (ureter, detrusor) smooth muscle relaxers mechanism block α1-adrenergic receptors → smooth muscle relaxation. the clinically useful effect is at α1a (prostate/bladder neck → opens the outlet). the unwanted effect is at α1b (vasculature → vasodilation → hypotension). newer "uroselective" agents (tamsulosin, silodosin) target α1a preferentially; older ones (terazosin, doxazosin) hit α1b as well and drop blood pressure. indications bph-associated luts — first-line, mainstay. voiding trial after acute retention — improves the odds of a successful trial of void. medical expulsive therapy (met) for distal ureteric stones — best evidence for stones >5 mm at the uvj. female voiding dysfunction from primary bladder neck obstruction — off-label but used. agents drug dose notes tamsulosin 0.4 mg po daily (flomax cr: same time daily, with or without food) workhorse. α1a-selective. floppy-iris syndrome — flag for the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery. silodosin 8 mg po daily most α1a-selective. most ejaculatory dysfunction. least bp drop. alfuzosin 10 mg po daily less selective; tolerable bp profile. terazosin / doxazosin titrated up over weeks older, also antihypertensive. useful when you want both effects; otherwise tamsulosin is cleaner. side effects to flag orthostatic hypotension — first-dose phenomenon, worst with non-selective agents. take at bedtime. ejaculatory dysfunction — reduced or absent ejaculate (anejaculation), not true retrograde flow. common with tamsulosin, very common with silodosin. tell the patient before they take the first dose. intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (ifis) — applies to all but worst with tamsulosin. patients facing cataract surgery should tell their ophthalmologist. dizziness, nasal congestion, fatigue. the teaching point α1-blockers are dynamic — they relax tone. they don't shrink anything. effect is felt in days. if you stop them, the symptom returns within days. pair with a 5-ari when the prostate is large and the patient wants a chance at long-term independence from the medication. s 5

label: 5α-Reductase Inhibitors (5-ARIs)
text: 5α-reductase inhibitors (5-aris) · block conversion of testosterone → dihydrotestosterone (dht) prostate shrinkers mechanism dht is the androgen that drives prostatic glandular growth. 5α-reductase converts testosterone to dht. block the enzyme → dht falls by 70–90% → prostate volume falls by ~20–25% over 6–12 months. this is the static component of bph. indications bph with a large prostate (>30 ml on imaging, psa >1.5 ng/ml, or palpable enlargement on dre) — where actual gland reduction matters. reduction of acute urinary retention and bph-related surgery risk over the long term (combat, mtops data). hematuria of prostatic origin — reduces vascularity. off-label: androgenic alopecia (finasteride 1 mg). agents drug dose notes finasteride 5 mg po daily blocks type ii 5α-reductase. dutasteride 0.5 mg po daily blocks types i and ii. slightly greater dht suppression; clinically similar. side effects to flag sexual — decreased libido, ed, ejaculatory volume reduction. counsel before starting. gynecomastia, breast tenderness. psa reduction by ~50% after 6–12 months. always double the psa when interpreting in a patient on a 5-ari, and document the multiplier in the chart. failure to do this is a classic missed cancer. pregnancy hazard — absorbed drug can impair genital development in a male fetus. pregnant women (or those who may become pregnant) should not handle crushed or broken finasteride tablets or leaking dutasteride capsules. men on dutasteride must not donate blood for 6 months after the last dose. the teaching point 5-aris are structural — they shrink. effect is felt in months. the right patient is the one with the big prostate who can wait six months. the wrong patient is the man in acute retention asking what will help him void tomorrow — give him tamsulosin for that, and add a 5-ari if his prostate is large enough to benefit over time. tamsulosin is the now-drug. finasteride/dutasteride is the year-drug. s 3

label: Antimuscarinics (Anticholinergics)
text: antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) · m3 antagonism — detrusor (and salivary, gi, eye, brain) detrusor quieters mechanism the detrusor contracts via m3 muscarinic receptors. block them → fewer involuntary contractions → less urgency, less frequency, fewer urge-incontinence episodes. the cost is everywhere else muscarinic receptors live: salivary glands (dry mouth), gut (constipation), eye (blurry vision, raised iop in angle-closure glaucoma), brain (cognition). indications overactive bladder (oab) — urgency, frequency, urge incontinence — without significant outflow obstruction or retention. neurogenic detrusor overactivity — often higher doses. agents drug receptor selectivity notes oxybutynin (ir / er / transdermal) non-selective m1–m5 cheapest, most side effects. crosses bbb — worst for cognition. avoid in elderly. tolterodine non-selective but bladder-preferential better tolerated than oxybutynin ir. solifenacin m3-selective once daily. cleaner profile. darifenacin m3-selective less cns penetration; preferred in older patients if antimuscarinic is needed. trospium quaternary amine — minimal bbb crossing cognitive-sparing option. side effects to flag urinary retention. the same mechanism that quiets the detrusor in overactivity can paralyze it in someone with marginal voiding. do not give to a man with significant bph and high pvr. anticholinergic burden — sums with other anticholinergics (tcas, diphenhydramine, antipsychotics). the elderly patient on three of them is a delirium waiting for the trigger. acute angle-closure glaucoma — contraindicated. open-angle glaucoma is fine. cognitive decline — emerging long-term data, especially with oxybutynin. prefer β3 agonists in older patients when you can. the trap a man with frequency and urgency from bph-induced overflow can look like oab. treating him with an antimuscarinic before checking a pvr will tip him into frank retention. always check a pvr before starting an antimuscarinic in a man with luts. a pvr of 250–300 ml or more means stop and think: you're likely treating the wrong layer. s 3

label: β3-Adrenergic Agonists
text: β3-adrenergic agonists · β3 stimulation — detrusor smooth muscle relaxation (storage phase) detrusor relaxers mechanism the detrusor expresses β3-adrenergic receptors that, when stimulated, promote relaxation during the storage phase. activating them increases bladder capacity and decreases urgency without paralyzing detrusor contraction during voiding — which is the win over antimuscarinics. indications overactive bladder — alternative to antimuscarinics, especially in patients with cognitive concerns, dry mouth burden, or contraindications. combination therapy with an antimuscarinic for refractory oab (synergistic). agents drug dose notes mirabegron 25–50 mg po daily the original. modest bp elevation — check baseline bp, recheck after starting. vibegron — coming: not yet available in canada (under health canada review as of sept 2026). minimal bp signal in us data. side effects hypertension — modest, but real with mirabegron. avoid in uncontrolled htn. headache, nasopharyngitis, uti symptoms. drug interactions — mirabegron is a cyp2d6 inhibitor; raises metoprolol, some antidepressants. why this class exists antimuscarinics treat oab by paralyzing the detrusor everywhere. β3 agonists treat oab by relaxing the detrusor during storage without blocking its ability to contract for voiding. cleaner mechanism, cleaner side effect profile. they are the right starting choice in many older patients now, even though antimuscarinics remain cheaper and more familiar. s 5

label: PDE5 Inhibitors
text: pde5 inhibitors · block phosphodiesterase 5 → increased cgmp → vascular smooth muscle relaxation vascular relaxers mechanism nitric oxide → cgmp → smooth muscle relaxation. pde5 degrades cgmp. block pde5, cgmp rises, smooth muscle relaxes — specifically, the smooth muscle of the corpus cavernosum (erections), the prostate and bladder neck (bph symptoms), and the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary hypertension). indications erectile dysfunction — first-line oral therapy. bph-related luts (tadalafil 5 mg daily) — particularly when ed and bph coexist. pulmonary hypertension (different dosing, different formulation). agents drug onset / duration notes sildenafil 30–60 min onset, ~4 h duration take on empty stomach. bluish vision tinge (pde6 cross-reactivity). tadalafil 30 min, 24–36 h ("weekender") 5 mg daily for bph ± ed. once-daily dosing is the luts use. vardenafil / avanafil intermediate niche. critical contraindications nitrates — absolute contraindication. severe hypotension. includes sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain. a patient prescribed any nitrate — even prn nitroglycerin he never uses — must not be given a pde5i. the 24 h / 48 h rule runs the other way: if a man who took a pde5i then needs a nitrate in an emergency, wait ≥24 h after sildenafil/vardenafil or ≥48 h after tadalafil, and give it only with monitoring. α-blockers — relative; can synergize for hypotension. tamsulosin generally safe with pde5i at standard doses, but counsel on orthostasis. recent mi / unstable cardiac status — defer. severe hepatic impairment — tadalafil once-daily not recommended; on-demand only with caution. sildenafil: start low. side effects headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion. vision changes (sildenafil; rare ischemic optic neuropathy reported). priapism — rare; counsel patients to seek care at >4 hours. the teaching point sildenafil and tadalafil are the same mechanism with different pharmacokinetics. pick on the basis of patient preference, dosing pattern (event-driven vs. daily), and other indications (bph-coexistent ed → daily tadalafil is two diagnoses one pill). the danger is always nitrates. ask. twice. s 1·3·5

label: Antibiotics — Urologic Use
text: antibiotics — urologic use · pathogen and tissue penetration drive choice, not "broad-spectrum vs narrow" match site to drug match the antibiotic to the station site / scenario first-line why acute uncomplicated cystitis (bladder, station 3) nitrofurantoin 100 mg bid ×5 d or tmp-smx ds bid ×3 d or fosfomycin 3 g ×1 bladder-concentrating agents. nitrofurantoin doesn't reach renal tissue — perfect for cystitis, useless for pyelo. pyelonephritis (kidney, station 1) outpatient: ciprofloxacin 500 mg bid ×7 d (if local resistance low). inpatient: ceftriaxone 1 g iv, then tailor. renal tissue penetration required. never use nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for pyelo — they don't reach parenchymal tissue. acute bacterial prostatitis (prostate, station 5) ciprofloxacin or tmp-smx, 2–4 weeks lipid-soluble agents penetrate the inflamed prostate. β-lactams penetrate poorly when uninflamed; in acute prostatitis the barrier is leaky and most agents work — but the duration is what matters. chronic bacterial prostatitis fluoroquinolone 4–6 weeks lipid solubility is the only way through. β-lactams fail. urosepsis with obstruction pip-tazo or carbapenem empirically, plus drainage drainage is the procedure. antibiotics support it; they do not substitute for it. pre-procedure prophylaxis (cystoscopy, trus biopsy) per institutional protocol; rectal swab-guided for prostate biopsy transperineal biopsy is increasingly preferred because of its lower infection risk. if trus is used, give swab- or culture-guided prophylaxis — fluoroquinolone resistance has risen sharply. rules that get you 80% of the way nitrofurantoin is a bladder drug. useless for kidney, prostate, blood. useful and clean for uncomplicated cystitis. canadian monographs contraindicate it at crcl < 60 ml/min (eau/beers accept egfr ≥ 30); follow local stewardship guidance. fluoroquinolones penetrate everything urologic. including prostate. tendinopathy, dysglycemia, qt prolongation, c. difficile — reserve them. tmp-smx — good cystitis and prostate. watch creatinine bump (tubular secretion, usually not real aki), hyperkalemia, sulfa allergy. ceftriaxone — workhorse inpatient pyelonephritis empirically. easy iv-to-po once cultures back. always send the culture before the first dose when feasible. the culture is what tells you the second week. the asymptomatic bacteriuria rule positive urine culture, no symptoms, no fever, no pyuria-with-pain → do not treat . exceptions: pregnancy, pre-urologic procedure with mucosal trauma expected. treating colonization selects resistance, changes nothing clinically, and turns the next real infection harder to treat. this is the most violated rule in inpatient urinary management. don't be the one who violates it. s 6

label: Phenazopyridine & Desmopressin — Surface Agents
text: phenazopyridine & desmopressin — surface agents · one numbs symptom · one reduces urine production narrow uses phenazopyridine (pyridium) topical urinary analgesic. turns urine and tears bright orange — warn patients, warn the lab. treats nothing, masks dysuria. useful: short-term symptom relief in confirmed uncomplicated cystitis while antibiotics work, 2 days max. dangerous: in renal insufficiency or liver disease (both contraindications; methemoglobinemia, hemolytic anemia), as a substitute for actual diagnosis, or in patients with g6pd deficiency. desmopressin (ddavp) synthetic vasopressin analog. reduces nocturnal urine production. useful: primary nocturnal enuresis in children (oral forms only — intranasal is contraindicated for enuresis in canada), nocturnal polyuria in carefully selected adults, mild factor viii deficiency / von willebrand. hyponatremia is the dangerous side effect. restrict fluids around dosing. contraindicated with hyponatremia (current or past), crcl <50, cardiac insufficiency or diuretic need, siadh, and polydipsia. nocdurna: 25 µg women, 50 µg men. sodium must be normal before starting; in men 65+, recheck at 4–8 days and at 1 month. death from severe hyponatremia is documented and entirely preventable. why these get grouped here both feel innocuous and both cause serious harm when used carelessly. phenazopyridine is a band-aid that hides infection while it climbs. desmopressin is a powerful water-retainer in a population that often cannot tolerate it. treat both as prescribing decisions, not otc suggestions.

label: Two Quick Rules of Thumb
text: two quick rules of thumb · the "before you sign" checklist where along the tract is the problem? where along the tract does this drug work? is there a pvr i should know before starting it? (before antimuscarinics in anyone with obstructive symptoms — including most men with luts — neurologic disease, or prior prostate or incontinence surgery.) is the patient on nitrates? label: The Operations — What Actually Happens
text: the operations — what actually happens · five operations, each on one part of the urinary tract. what the surgeon physically does, what recovery after surgery should look like, and the complications you'll hear about on the call phone. for pas, medical students, and clinical clerks.

label: How To Read This Document
text: how to read this document · every operation has the same shape, and we describe each in that shape. which part of the urinary tract does it work on? what does it remove or rearrange? what should recovery look like, day by day? what complications bring the patient back, and which need urology vs. emergency surgery vs. medicine? the point isn't to make you a surgeon. the point is so that when a post-op patient calls or returns and the chart says "pod3 s/p holep" (post-op day 3 after a holep), you have a picture in your head of what was just done to that man's prostate, what his urine should look like today, and what would worry the surgeon enough that you should call. three kinds of operation every urology operation either removes something that's blocking or diseased , rebuilds a section of the tract , or creates a new exit when the existing one cannot work . keep those three kinds in mind and you can roughly predict how any patient will recover.

label: 1 — TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate)
text: 1 — turp (transurethral resection of the prostate) · 5 station

label: TURP
text: turp · prostate (station 5) · bph outlet obstruction · endoscopic remove what the operation is removing. the hyperplastic adenoma (yellow) compresses the prostatic urethra and bulges into the bladder neck. resection or enucleation removes that mass and re-opens the channel through the prostate (station 5), leaving the true prostatic capsule behind. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract . what the surgeon actually does a resectoscope passes up the urethra to the prostate. a wire loop carries cutting current and shaves the obstructing adenoma — the inner zone of the prostate — into small chips, which are irrigated out and sent to pathology. the capsule, the verumontanum, and the external sphincter are preserved. hemostasis is the other half of the operation; bleeding from the prostatic fossa is brisk if not controlled. at the end, a 22 fr 3-way foley with cbi sits in the bladder. standard post-op course pod 0 3-way foley with cbi. urine pink to light red, never bright red. patient may have bladder spasms — antimuscarinic prn (oxybutynin; b&o suppositories are no longer marketed in canada). hgb checked overnight. pod 1 cbi off if urine pink, bpl irrigation as needed. diet advanced. ambulate. most patients go home pod 1 with the catheter still in. pod 1–3 catheter out in clinic or at home with pcp support. patient may have dysuria, urgency, frequency for 2–4 weeks ("raw fossa healing"). coach: drink water, avoid caffeine, expect intermittent pink urine at terminal stream for weeks. weeks 2–6 delayed bleeding is the classic visit — eschar sloughs off the resected fossa around pod 10–21 and patients see frank blood. usually self-limited with hydration; escalate if clot retention or hemodynamic change. complications that come back to you clot retention — most common urgent return. manual evacuation + cbi restart. see procedures doc. delayed hematuria at week 2–3 — eschar sloughing. usually clears with hydration; call urology if it doesn't. uti — common, send culture, treat. tur syndrome (now rare) — historic complication of monopolar turp with hypotonic irrigation, causing hyponatremia and confusion. bipolar turp and holep use saline and have largely eliminated this. still worth knowing the term. retrograde ejaculation — expected, not a complication per se. pre-op counseling. permanent in roughly 50–70%. erectile dysfunction — risk discussed, but trials show erectile function is generally unchanged after turp; ejaculation is what changes. bladder neck contracture / urethral stricture — late complication, weeks to months. returns with worsening flow. persistent urinary incontinence — should be transient. persistent stress incontinence after 3 months suggests sphincter injury; call. things that should not happen — call now bright red effluent on cbi that doesn't clear with rate increase + manual evacuation. hemodynamic change with hematuria. inability to replace a dislodged foley in the first 48 hours — call before forcing. fever >38.5°c with rigors — urosepsis suspected.

label: 2 — HoLEP (Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate)
text: 2 — holep (holmium laser enucleation of the prostate) · 5 station

label: HoLEP
text: holep · prostate (station 5) · bph · endoscopic · laser enucleation + morcellation remove what's different from turp same target — the obstructing adenoma in the prostate (station 5) — but a different mechanical approach. the holmium laser develops a plane between the adenoma and the surgical capsule (the same plane an open simple prostatectomy uses), the adenoma is enucleated whole into the bladder, and a morcellator inside the bladder breaks it into pieces for removal. the result is more complete removal of adenoma than turp — including very large glands (>100 g) that previously required open surgery. hemostasis is excellent because the laser seals as it cuts. standard post-op course pod 0 3-way foley with cbi, typically lower irrigation rate than turp — less bleeding. often discharge same day in selected centers. pod 1 catheter out, void trial, discharge. faster than turp. first 2 weeks mild dysuria, urge, and possible stress urinary incontinence (transient, mechanism: the external sphincter has just lost its proximal support; trigone control returns within weeks). pelvic floor exercises help. weeks 2–4 symptoms continue improving. flow rates by week 4 are dramatically better than baseline. complications that come back to you early stress urinary incontinence — distinguishing feature from turp. patients leak on cough/exercise for weeks. reassure, refer to pelvic floor pt. most resolve by 3 months. hematuria — less than turp but still present. delayed eschar sloughing at week 2–3 still occurs. uti, urgency, retrograde ejaculation — similar to turp. bladder injury from the morcellator — rare; pre-empted by the surgeon, but if you see hematuria with peritonitis signs early post-op, this is the one to consider. the choice between turp and holep same target. turp is faster to teach, faster to perform on smaller glands, ubiquitously available. holep works on any prostate size, gives more complete tissue removal, and has the bleeding profile to handle anticoagulated patients. for glands >80 g, holep (or simple prostatectomy) is the right operation.

label: 3 — Ureteroscopy (URS) ± Holmium Lithotripsy + Stent
text: 3 — ureteroscopy (urs) ± holmium lithotripsy + stent · 2 station

label: Ureteroscopy
text: ureteroscopy · ureter (station 2) · stones, strictures, upper-tract tumors remove + bridge what the surgeon actually does a flexible (or semi-rigid) ureteroscope passes up the urethra, through the bladder, into the ureter through the uvj. the stone is visualized; a holmium laser breaks it into dust or small fragments; a basket retrieves the bigger pieces. a double-j ureteral stent is usually left in place at the end (it may be omitted after uncomplicated urs) to ensure drainage through the next 1–14 days while edema resolves. the stent has a loop at the renal pelvis and a loop at the bladder, holding it in. standard post-op course pod 0 same-day discharge in most cases. foley out before discharge. patient takes home a stent. days 1–7 stent symptoms: urgency, frequency, hematuria, suprapubic discomfort, flank pain on voiding (vesicoureteral reflux up the stent). all expected. phenazopyridine prn for dysuria. α-blocker (tamsulosin) sometimes improves stent tolerance. push fluids. days 7–14 stent removal in clinic — simple cystoscopic procedure. symptoms resolve within 24–48 hours of removal. weeks 4–6 repeat imaging (kub or ct) to confirm stone clearance. metabolic stone workup if recurrent. complications that come back to you stent symptoms more severe than expected — first thing: confirm the stent isn't migrated (kub). then anticholinergic + α-blocker + phenazopyridine. early stent removal if intractable. fever post-urs — assume infected obstruction until proven otherwise. ua, culture, cbc, lactate. ct if hydronephrosis suspected (stent should be preventing this — if hydronephrosis is present, the stent is occluded or displaced). forgotten stent — the classic late catastrophe. every stent has a planned removal date — usually 1–2 weeks after routine urs, within 14 days if the string is left on, and never past the device's labelled limit. encrusted stents that have been in for months become a stone surrounding a stent, removal becomes a major operation, and patients can lose renal function. track every stent you place. ureteral injury / perforation — rare; intraoperative finding usually. post-op presentation: persistent flank pain, urinoma on imaging. hematuria — pink urine for days is expected. frank red blood with clots is not. the stent counseling moment every patient who goes home with a stent gets one sentence drilled into them: "you have a plastic tube in your kidney. if you don't come back to have it taken out, you will lose this kidney." the number of patients lost to follow-up after stent placement is non-trivial. build a tracking system. confirm the removal appointment exists before they leave.

label: 4 — Robotic Radical Prostatectomy (RARP)
text: 4 — robotic radical prostatectomy (rarp) · 5 station

label: Robotic Radical Prostatectomy
text: robotic radical prostatectomy · prostate (station 5) · localized prostate cancer · oncologic resection + reconstruction remove + reconstruct why this operation exists. early prostate cancer (left) is contained within the gland — surgically curable. advanced disease (right) invades into bladder and beyond. radical prostatectomy is the curative option for organ-confined disease; locally advanced disease is treated multimodally. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract . what the surgeon actually does this is a different operation from turp/holep. those leave the prostate behind and just remove the obstructing inner zone. here, the entire prostate gland is removed, plus the seminal vesicles, plus a margin around the apex and base. the bladder neck is reconstructed and anastomosed directly to the urethra over a foley. pelvic lymphadenectomy is performed for staging in many cases. the patient leaves the or with a urethral foley sitting through a fresh anastomosis — that catheter is the operation until the anastomosis heals. standard post-op course pod 0–1 inpatient overnight in most centers; discharge pod 1 typical. foley to gravity, ambulate, diet advanced. drain (if placed) measured for output and creatinine. days 1–7 home with the foley. strict no-instrumentation: any urethral manipulation can disrupt the anastomosis. patient is taught foley care, leg bag use, and when to call. day 7–10 cystogram in clinic if surgeon protocol requires; if no leak, foley out. some surgeons remove without imaging. weeks 1–3 after foley out significant urinary incontinence — this is the expected price. the internal sphincter is gone (it was part of the prostate). continence depends on the external sphincter alone. pelvic floor pt starts immediately. most men (about 85–95% in published series) achieve continence by 12 months. months 1–3 first psa. should be undetectable (<0.1 ng/ml). rising psa = biochemical recurrence; oncology pathway. months 3–24 erectile function recovery — slower than continence. depends on nerve-sparing technique, age, baseline function. complications that come back to you catheter falls out / pulled in the first 7 days — do not replace blindly. call urology immediately. often requires cystoscopic placement over a wire to avoid disrupting the anastomosis. anastomotic leak — drain output that's urinous, drain creatinine markedly higher than serum. usually heals with prolonged foley drainage and a percutaneous drain. rarely re-operative. lymphocele — fluid collection in the pelvis from disrupted lymphatics. most asymptomatic and resolve. infected lymphocele or compressive lymphocele needs drainage. stress urinary incontinence at 3+ months — expected to varying degrees. persistent sui at 12 months may need surgical management (sling, aus). bladder neck contracture — late complication, narrows the anastomosis. returns with weak stream. erectile dysfunction — expected; managed with pde5i, vacuum devices, intracavernosal injections, eventually penile implant if refractory. rising psa — never normal after rp. >0.2 with confirmation = biochemical recurrence. the post-prostatectomy rule a post-prostatectomy patient with a foley problem in the first 30 days belongs on the operating surgeon's phone. not a generic urology consult. not the ed's catheter cart. the surgeon knows what their anastomosis looks like.

label: 5 — Partial Nephrectomy (Robotic or Open)
text: 5 — partial nephrectomy (robotic or open) · 1 station

label: Partial Nephrectomy
text: partial nephrectomy · kidney (station 1) · small renal masses · nephron-sparing remove + reconstruct the architecture being preserved. partial nephrectomy resects a tumor with a margin and reconstructs the cortex and collecting system back together. done well, this preserves nephrons (cortex/medulla mass) and renal function that radical nephrectomy would sacrifice. from burroughs wellcome co., atlas of the urinary tract . what the surgeon actually does the renal hilum is exposed. the renal artery is temporarily clamped (warm ischemia) — the clock starts. the tumor is excised with a small rim of normal parenchyma. the collecting system is closed (if entered). the cortex is reconstructed. the clamp comes off and the kidney reperfuses. the goal: tumor out, collecting system watertight, parenchyma reconstructed, kidney still working. standard post-op course pod 0–1 inpatient. jp drain in the perinephric space. foley overnight. hgb trended. creatinine bumped (expected — single-kidney ischemia time). pod 2–3 foley out. drain output trends: if low and serous, drain comes out before discharge. if high or urinous, drain stays. discharge pod 2–4 typically. weeks 1–4 recovery. restrictions on heavy lifting. watch for delayed bleeding (week 2–3 — pseudoaneurysm rupture territory). month 3, then annually surveillance imaging (ct or mri). renal function monitoring. complications that come back to you urine leak — drain output stays elevated, drain creatinine markedly higher than serum. confirm with drain cr. management: prolonged drain + foley to lower bladder pressure, ± ureteral stent to decompress upstream. most heal in weeks. reoperation rare. delayed bleeding (pseudoaneurysm rupture) — pod 7–21. sudden flank pain, hematuria, hemodynamic change. ct angio, ir embolization. this is a true emergency — recognize the timeline. aki — expected mild rise. significant aki suggests vascular injury, particularly if the patient has a solitary kidney or pre-existing ckd. positive surgical margin — pathology finding. surveillance vs. completion nephrectomy decision is the surgeon's, not ed's. wound infection / hernia at port site — standard surgical complications. why this operation exists instead of radical for small renal masses (<7 cm, t1), partial nephrectomy gives equivalent cancer control to radical nephrectomy and preserves nephrons. preserved nephrons matter long-term — less chronic kidney disease. a survival benefit is suggested by observational data but was not shown in the one randomized trial. partial is preferred for ct1a and, when feasible, t1b; radical keeps a role for complex tumors or higher oncologic risk.
